newsitem.title: USA: Sliding prompt crudes deflate WTI, grades advance.
newsitem.headline: Sliding prompt crudes deflate WTI, grades advance.

text.p: Sliding front month NYMEX paper crude prices deflated benchmark cash crudes in the U.S. Gulf Thursday afternoon, but grade barrels continued to stake firmer differentials on refiner buy moves.
July West Texas Intermediate/Cushing stood 15 cents weaker at $18.70-80 a barrel, figuring a 10 cents premium for cash over screen paper quotes on Exchange for Physical values.
Outright prices have found technical selling pressure since morning, lopping off 10-12 cents more than August declines, leaving the July/August roll around -12 cents.

Markets noticed, but failed to rally higher on a diplomatic tussle underway at the United Nations. Both the U.S. and British delegations came out in favor of imposing new sanctions on Iraq for blocking U.N. weapons inspection teams from sites in June.
Further consultations will resume Friday, but the state of the dialogue pits the U.S. and U.K. against China, Russia and other key Security Council states who don't favor increased sanctions.

At issue is the American and British draft resolution to reprimand Baghdad by preventing Iraqi government officials, members of the army and police and their immediate families from travelling abroad. The draft also calls for a suspension of sanctions reviews until Baghdad offers full cooperation with U.N. Special Commission inspection teams.

Back in the cash crude world, traders were more attuned to the newfound strength in grade differentials. Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James moved to positive price territory against benchmark WTI/Cushing on refiner position-squaring.
Refiners have spent much of June waiting for North Sea Brent cargoes to flood the Gulf, but the narrowed arbitrage and other factors squelched those expectations.
Other grades firmed as well, led by West Texas Sour/Midland where deals were done at low $1.20-25 discounts to the cash marker.
Still, cash traders said there are sweet West African and a slew of Latin American sours available for purchase.
"There is no problem with finding the crude. People just got caught with their positioning, this isn't a huge fundamental shift," said a cash trader.
